pi.name: Erik Nielsen
pi.title: Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Erik Nielsen earned his Ph.D. in 1997 from the Plant Research Lab at Michigan State University and was a postdoctoral fellow at EMBL Heidelberg, Germany, from 1998 to 2001. He is a Professor in the Department of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology at the University of Michigan. His research examines polarized secretion during cellular differentiation, focusing on the membrane trafficking pathways that deliver cell wall components in plants and how this relates to plant growth and development.

lab_description: The Nielsen Lab investigates plant cell wall biosynthesis in Arabidopsis thaliana, exploring the cell biology underlying this essential process, which is crucial for plant growth, development, and defense. The lab uses genetic, biochemical, and live-cell imaging techniques to study the cellular and molecular mechanisms of cell wall formation, with emphasis on how cellulose synthase (CESA) and cellulose synthase-like D (CSLD) proteins are sorted and delivered to specific plasma membrane domains during polarized growth. Additional work examines KORRIGAN accessory proteins that regulate cellulose synthase activity and how plants sense and respond to artificial nanomaterials derived from cell wall fractions.

research_areas.title: Cellulose synthesis protein sorting
research_areas.summary: Identifies how CESA and CSLD proteins are delivered to specific plasma membrane domains, including CSLD3 as a beta-1,4-glucan synthase in tip-growing cells and CSLD5 in cell plate formation.

research_areas.title: KORRIGAN proteins
research_areas.summary: Investigates accessory proteins that regulate cellulose synthase activity during cell wall synthesis.

research_areas.title: Plant responses to nanomaterials
research_areas.summary: Studies how plants sense and respond to artificial nanomaterials derived from cell wall fractions, in the context of agricultural nanotechnology.
